items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: He booked Roy Eldridge, he booked Charlie Shavers, he booked Buck Clayton, Bobby Hackett, Billy Butterfield.

ctx.x: Right. That’s a heck of a good start. I wanted to ask you about — I guess this would be sort of a current question. I’ve had some conversations recently with a professor about women in jazz. And I wonder if you have any thoughts about the question of why isn’t there more?

Well it’s a good question, I’m glad you asked it, because it is something that is on my mind. We know that historically there’ve been certain important women in jazz — certainly the singers, but then there’s Mary Lou Williams who is always brought up as the great female arranger, composer and instrumentalist. But although there were some very talented women, a lot of piano players but also horn players, it really was a minority. I remember seeing — Charlie Shavers brought a group into a little club in New York…

attractive lady. And she played great bass. But that was such a novelty. And today fortunately we have a lot more talented and fairly prominent women in jazz. I mean I was a big fan of hers anyway but I was very happy when Anat Cohen started winning the clarinet thing in the DownBeat Critics Poll and has won it over a number of years. She also came very close to being musician of the year. She was like second a few years ago. But there are others. Ingrid Jensen is a very good trumpet player, Virginia Mayhew is an…

ctx.x: Yeah. He became a Billy Graham accolade. But that was another side. Lonnie was a pretty good piano player. He would occasionally – very rarely he might sit in on a jam session. He had been to New England Conservatory. He was a talented composer. Lonnie’s still around. He’s older than me. He’s now in his 80s. Except for a brief period, when he was associated with Charlie Mingus and made an album on Mingus’s Debut label which has never been reissued, but one track was reissued in this big Debut CD package which…

Floyd Campbell on washboard, Buster Bailey on clarinet, and James P. Johnson on piano. That was an incredible thing to see in the late 1940s, early 1950s. It was already a chunk of bygone history. All sorts of people that he would have. He seemed to know everybody. Then a few years later, after I got back out of the Army – we’ll come to that later – when I was hanging out at the Copper Rail in mid-Manhattan, one day suddenly Bob Maltz came in and said, “Has anybody seen Art Blakey?” That seemed like such a…
